title: Plans, intentions and invitations
summary: Make the volitional form ('let's'), say what you're thinking of doing, what you intend to do and what is scheduled, and review polite invitations with {ませんか} and {ましょう}.

points.title: Volitional form (〜う / 〜よう)
points.structure: る-verb: drop る + よう (食[た]べよう) / う-verb: o-sound + う (行[い]こう) / する → しよう, 来[く]る → 来[こ]よう

examples.jp: 疲[つか]れたね。ちょっと休[やす]もう。
examples.en: I'm tired. Let's take a little break.

examples.jp: 明日[あした]は早[はや]いから、もう寝[ね]よう。
examples.en: I have an early start tomorrow, so I'll go to bed now.

examples.jp: 暑[あつ]いね。何[なに]か冷[つめ]たいものを飲[の]もうか。
examples.en: It's hot, isn't it. Shall we drink something cold?

examples.jp: 週末[しゅうまつ]、一緒[いっしょ]に映画[えいが]を見[み]に行[い]こうよ。
examples.en: Let's go see a movie together this weekend!

examples.jp: 荷物[にもつ]、一[ひと]つ持[も]とうか。
examples.en: Shall I carry one of your bags?

points.notes: Only use the volitional with actions you can choose to do. Verbs like {分[わ]かる} or {ある}, and potential forms, don't have a meaningful volitional.

quiz.q: 雨[あめ]が降[ふ]ってきたから、早[はや]く＿＿。
quiz.en: It's started raining, so let's hurry home.

quiz.q: 今日[きょう]は私[わたし]が晩[ばん]ご飯[はん]を＿＿か。

points.title: 〜ようと思[おも]う
points.meaning: I think I'll ~ / I'm thinking of ~ing
points.structure: V-volitional + と思[おも]う / と思[おも]っている
points.explanation:
Volitional + {と思[おも]う} literally means 'I think, "let's do ~"' — in other words, 'I think I'll ~'. It's the most common way to talk about your plans in a soft, not-yet-fixed way.

- {と思[おも]います}: a decision you're making right now. {今日[きょう]は早[はや]く寝[ね]ようと思[おも]います} 'I think I'll go to bed early tonight.'
- {と思[おも]っています}: an intention you've had for a while. {来年[らいねん]、日本[にほん]で働[はたら]こうと思[おも]っています} 'I'm planning to work in Japan next year.'

The plain {と思[おも]う} form only describes your own intentions. To talk about someone else's plans, use {と思[おも]っている}: {兄[あに]は車[くるま]を買[か]おうと思[おも]っています} 'My brother is thinking of buying a car.'

examples.jp: 今年[ことし]の夏[なつ]、日本[にほん]へ行[い]こうと思[おも]っています。
examples.en: I'm thinking of going to Japan this summer.

examples.jp: 今日[きょう]は疲[つか]れたので、早[はや]く寝[ね]ようと思[おも]います。
examples.en: I'm tired today, so I think I'll go to bed early.

examples.jp: 兄[あに]は新[あたら]しい車[くるま]を買[か]おうと思[おも]っています。
examples.en: My older brother is thinking of buying a new car.

examples.jp: 大学[だいがく]を卒業[そつぎょう]した後[あと]、日本[にほん]で働[はたら]こうと思[おも]っています。
examples.en: After I graduate from university, I'm planning to work in Japan.

points.notes: There's no negative volitional in everyday use, so for 'I'm thinking of not ~ing' say {〜のはやめようと思[おも]う} ('I think I'll stop ~') or use {〜ないつもりだ} (next point).

quiz.q: 週末[しゅうまつ]は部屋[へや]の掃除[そうじ]を＿＿と思[おも]っています。
quiz.en: I'm planning to clean my room this weekend.

quiz.q: 来年[らいねん]、日本語[にほんご]の試験[しけん]を＿＿と思[おも]います。
quiz.en: I think I'll take the Japanese exam next year.

points.title: 〜つもりだ
points.structure: V-dictionary + つもりだ / V-ない + つもりだ
points.explanation:
{つもり} means 'intention'. {V + つもりだ} says you have firmly decided to do something — it's stronger and more settled than {〜ようと思[おも]う}. {夏休[なつやす]みは国[くに]へ帰[かえ]るつもりです} 'I intend to go back to my country for the summer holidays.'

For 'intend not to', put the verb in the {ない}-form: {もうたばこは吸[す]わないつもりだ} 'I don't intend to smoke anymore.' The form {〜つもりはない} is stronger still: 'I have no intention whatsoever of ~'.

You can ask friends {〜つもり？}, but asking a superior directly about their intentions can sound a bit intrusive. With people above you, it's more polite to ask about their {予定[よてい]} (next point).

examples.jp: 夏休[なつやす]みは国[くに]へ帰[かえ]るつもりです。
examples.en: I intend to go back to my country for the summer holidays.

examples.jp: もうたばこは吸[す]わないつもりだ。
examples.en: I don't intend to smoke anymore.

examples.jp: 今日[きょう]はどこにも出[で]かけないつもりです。
examples.en: I'm not planning to go out anywhere today.

examples.jp: 日本[にほん]に何年[なんねん]ぐらい住[す]むつもりですか。
examples.en: About how many years do you intend to live in Japan?

examples.jp: 彼[かれ]と結婚[けっこん]するつもりはありません。
examples.en: I have no intention of marrying him.

points.notes: Past + {つもり} has a different meaning, 'I thought I had ~': {鍵[かぎ]をかけたつもりだった} 'I thought I had locked it (but I hadn't)'.

quiz.q: 来月[らいげつ]、新[あたら]しいパソコンを＿＿つもりです。
quiz.en: I intend to buy a new computer next month.

quiz.q: 体[からだ]に悪[わる]いから、もうお酒[さけ]は＿＿つもりです。
quiz.en: It's bad for my health, so I intend not to drink alcohol anymore.

points.title: 〜予定[よてい]だ
points.structure: V-dictionary + 予定[よてい]だ / Noun + の + 予定[よてい]だ
points.explanation:
{予定[よてい]} means 'schedule' or 'plan'. {V + 予定[よてい]だ} says something is arranged — it's on the calendar. Unlike {つもり}, which is about your personal will, {予定[よてい]} is about arrangements, often involving other people, timetables or organisations: meetings, flights, trips, events.

{会議[かいぎ]は三時[さんじ]に始[はじ]まる予定[よてい]です} 'The meeting is scheduled to start at three.' A plane can have a {予定[よてい]}, but it can't have a {つもり}!

With a noun, add {の}: {出張[しゅっちょう]の予定[よてい]です} 'I'm scheduled for a business trip.' {予定[よてい]} is also a normal noun: {週末[しゅうまつ]は予定[よてい]がありますか} 'Do you have plans this weekend?'

examples.jp: 会議[かいぎ]は三時[さんじ]に始[はじ]まる予定[よてい]です。
examples.en: The meeting is scheduled to start at three.

examples.jp: 来週[らいしゅう]、大阪[おおさか]へ出張[しゅっちょう]の予定[よてい]です。
examples.en: I'm scheduled to go on a business trip to Osaka next week.

examples.jp: 週末[しゅうまつ]は何[なに]か予定[よてい]がありますか。
examples.en: Do you have any plans for the weekend?

examples.jp: 新[あたら]しい駅[えき]は来年[らいねん]できる予定[よてい]です。
examples.en: The new station is scheduled to open next year.

examples.jp: 飛行機[ひこうき]は七時[しちじ]に着[つ]く予定[よてい]でしたが、一時間[いちじかん]遅[おく]れました。
examples.en: The plane was scheduled to arrive at seven, but it was an hour late.

points.notes: Quick comparison: {〜ようと思[おも]う} = thinking about it; {〜つもり} = I've made up my mind; {〜予定[よてい]} = it's arranged / on the schedule.

quiz.q: 飛行機[ひこうき]は十時[じゅうじ]に出[で]る＿＿です。
quiz.en: The plane is scheduled to depart at ten.

quiz.q: 来月[らいげつ]、東京[とうきょう]で友[とも]だちの結婚式[けっこんしき]＿＿予定[よてい]です。
quiz.en: My friend's wedding is scheduled for next month in Tokyo.

points.title: 〜ませんか / 〜ましょう / 〜ましょうか (review)
points.structure: V-ます stem + ませんか / ましょう / ましょうか
points.explanation:
Three polite endings you already know, now side by side:

- {〜ませんか} 'Won't you ~? / Would you like to ~?' The softest invitation; it leaves the other person room to say no. Best for a first invitation.
- {〜ましょう} 'Let's ~.' Use it once you both agree, or when you're enthusiastic. As a first invitation it can sound a bit pushy.
- {〜ましょうか} 'Shall I ~? / Shall we ~?' Used for offers ({持[も]ちましょうか} 'Shall I carry it?') and for deciding details together ({何時[なんじ]に会[あ]いましょうか} 'What time shall we meet?').

The casual versions are {〜ない？} ({飲[の]まない？}), the volitional ({飲[の]もう}), and volitional + {か} ({飲[の]もうか}).

To decline politely, Japanese people rarely say a flat 'no'. Try {すみません、その日[ひ]はちょっと…}.

examples.jp: 今度[こんど]の土曜日[どようび]、一緒[いっしょ]に食事[しょくじ]をしませんか。
examples.en: Would you like to have a meal together this Saturday?

examples.jp: いいですね。じゃあ、駅[えき]の前[まえ]で会[あ]いましょう。
examples.en: Sounds good. Then let's meet in front of the station.

examples.jp: 寒[さむ]いですね。窓[まど]を閉[し]めましょうか。
examples.en: It's cold, isn't it. Shall I close the window?

examples.jp: 何時[なんじ]に出[で]かけましょうか。
examples.en: What time shall we head out?

examples.jp: ねえ、コーヒー飲[の]まない？
examples.en: Hey, want to get a coffee?

quiz.q: 重[おも]いですね。一[ひと]つ＿＿。
quiz.en: That's heavy, isn't it. Shall I carry one?

quiz.q: あのう、今晩[こんばん]、一緒[いっしょ]に飲[の]みに行[い]き＿＿。
quiz.en: Um, would you like to go for a drink together tonight?
